comments.name: Perspective

Siblings jostle & joust in play throughout the animal kingdom. Independence (& estrangement) is a normal stage of development. The key to understanding sibling conflict is how their parents related to each individual & the perception of this by each sibling.

comments.name: Diogenes
comments.body:
I have given a lot of tbought to my struggles in a relationship with a younger brother and have come to three things that had created distance between us:

1. Differences in personality and temperament. Conservative and structured vs. free spirited & wild.
2. Contest for primacy in the family.  Who is the most important? Who has power?
3. Our parents treatment of him, particularly from our mother. At birth, he almost died, giving her a life-long, deep anxiety about him, a well-documented fact about parents who nearly lose a child. My resentment of that attention.

Now that we are old & our parents are gone, I am able to see why friction occurred. I'm past that. Life is too brief. Your sibling is your shared history.

comments.name: Kiwi
comments.body: Such a great piece. I'm glad to see sibling therapy is on the rise; I'd like to do it. One thing that I think is worth discussing much bigger here, though, is what responsibility we place on kids, especially young kids. Daniel takes the blame in several instances here, but a kid is often just the messenger for a family's dysfunction, not the bringer of it. What forces compelled him into such competition with his brother? He can own his childhood part now, and how that might have affected Bob, but some of that also deserves fair context.

She laughed. She has lied to my other sister about her behavior towards me. On several occasions she has cut off communication, most recently 3 years ago. It was stressful, since we were working on how to manage our mother's dementia, selling her house, divesting the furnishings, etc. My brother and I took a step back, didn't take anything because we knew there would be comments about how much we have compared to her situation. She left that last day we were all together without saying goodbye, changed her phone number and left no forwarding address. The story is much longer than can be described in this little box, but suffice it to say, after being harangued, sworn at,  had more invective thrown at me, I am not interested in reconnecting.

This isn't straightforward. There are two issues discussed here, sexual harassment on the job; and. racial, ethnic and gender discrimination in hiring and promotion

The government's Investigation and prosecution of gender., ethnic, and racial discrimination on the job has often been excessive, unfair, and counterproductive. A common criteria used by many government enforcement agencies has been disparate impact, that is the evaluation of employer job statistics to confirm that the numbers of employees, categorized by. race, ethnicity, or gender, match the population at large. Though this is often allowed by law, it may well violate the Constitution. In practice, disparate impact replaces merit-based employment practices with quota driven processes. President Trump is correct to try to eliminate the use of disparate impact.

Sexual harassment on the workplace and a toxic work environment are the second issue discussed in this article. Many of the complaints described ring true and it is the role of the government to investigate, prevent, and, when appropriate, punish employers who tolerate a toxic work environment. Not all allegations are true, and there are a minority of employees who exploit their sexuality inappropriately on the job, but most of the allegations presented in this article seem real, and President Trump should not interfere with investigation by appropriate federal agencies.

That distinction matters in a replacement process like this, where internal party committees — not independent groups — ultimately determine the nominee.

China's open-source approach is not a matter of an authoritarian state ironically defying its evil nature, but, as is often the case, of a successful, independent state defying US stereotypes.

In the days before AC, standard male dress in British tropical colonies consisted of short-sleeved shirts, "tailored" (as they called them) shorts, knee socks -- and sometimes a necktie.  The look hung on in a few places (back in the 80s as a  banker, I paid a call on  a government office in Darwin, Australia and that's how  the men were dressed.)
 Baden-Powell outfitted his newly established Boy Scouts in this style -- soon copied by elite British schools -- and then in Japan  in an era when Japan looked to Britain as a model.  The outfit  became standard wear for Japanese grade school boys.  But shorts  acquired a "boys clothes'' aura so you got the absurdity of grade school boys required to wear shorts in the mid-winter while their older brothers sweated in regulation long trousers in  mid-summer and no Japanese man would ever wear shorts except at the beach or the gym.   That's been changing -- and it's good thing. It's perfectly possible -- as the photos accompanying the article demonstrate  -- to look appropriately serious for an office environment while dressed in neat shorts and short-sleeved shirts.  The Brits managed it a century ago in the Federated Malay States and it wouldn't surprise me to see the fashion-forward Japanese bringing on an updated version of menswear that is both sensible for hot, humid weather and allows the wearer to look professional.

My music news website has lost up to 80 percent of its referral traffic this year as Google promotes AI over sites in its search results. Meanwhile, our stories — many of which are created from our own reporting and print archive — are helping to inform the very AI results that are promoted over our web pages. 

But AI is only one side of the story. Since the start of 2026, Google has also made it harder for sites to have their stories picked up in Discover, the personalized content feed where it pushes recommended stories to users. In the past, Discover has increased referral traffic on some of our stories by up to 500 percent. The sudden decline in Discover has wiped out our gains and imperiled jobs.  

Google is an independent business and entitled to its decisions. But it is benefitting from the independent reporting and research created and paid for by others, and promoting itself at their expense. That is simply unfair. 

Regulation might help, but before that happens I think more websites will move their content to apps, email newsletters and anywhere else Google can't reach. The days of free access to information are coming to an end.

comments.name: Best Guess
comments.body:
The only chatbot I have to interact with is Strava.  It gives me praise for riding faster .

It encourages 'weekly goals'.  It offers to 'tell me more.'  It does not get upset that I rebuff its advances every time.

Then, the app is ready to track many stats: Power, heartbeat, VO2 max, cadence, calories burned. 
It wants me to rate 'how the ride felt.' It probably would like to check my muscle density and suggest I change diet.

I am starting to wonder why I pay it.  And, who sets its expectations about what is good.  It needs to have a priorities synthesiser like old time sound mixers;  I don't need to improve.  Just stay able to ride.  I don't want a love affair with my phone.  

I do like how it sums up the ride, distilling the pace and distance into a few sentences.  At my age, the records do not get better; they maintain or get slower.  The excitement of seeing my PR's and the standing on the leaderboard has been replaced by 'I could just use my cyclocomputer to track this and no one would know my ride.' But, the people I ride with are all on it,  I see their efforts and they mine.  I like to see their pictures.  When the subscription runs out, I will wait for the discount offer then sign up for another year.  But not for 'tell me more.'  

Here is to hoping that the dopamine hit loses its power for the younger generation, who do not know what driving across the country with only a map, asking directions, and asking people is like, nor will ever know. .

Moreover, we seem to have lost our connection to the most critical and powerful life tool...experience.

Life is about experience. Learning is about experience. Love is about experience. Relationships are about experience. 

Maturity and wisdom are a result of - you guessed it - experience.

Too much time on - and attachment to - technology is robbing us of the most precious and powerful life tool we have access to...experience.

If you think this is too simple, too unsphhisticated, step back for a moment and just...think about it.

Think about it purely from common sense...

...not from media, marketing, advertising, technology, social media, politics, or consumerism...Just. Common. Sense.

Time on technology - engaging with A.I., ChatGPT, ChatBots, etc. - doesn't provide you tangible experience.

And that is why we are here...to have a human expereince with ourselves and with one another.

That is, actually, how human beings evolve...expereince.

We are physical beings in a physical body, in a physical world...our "physics" matters most.

That's not "woo-woo," it's common sense; of which we now have a dearth of...predominantly due to the over-use of technology.

We have made our "tools" our master. 

Time to take our power - and our humanity - back.

What is less well known is that the anti-Catholic penal laws also applied to Protestant Dissenters such as Presbyterians, all be it to a lesser extent, especially those in the province of Ulster in Ireland.
 
It was one of the push factors that drove hundreds of thousands of Irish Presbyterians to emigrate to North America in the 1700s before the American revolution.

Seems like the time in Iten was well spent, learning to simplify things and to train with the "listen to your body" mantra top of mind at all times. Distance running is as much a mental challenge as it is a physical endeavour, and learning how to relax while running takes a lot of time and practice, and eventually allows you to retain your form longer, which in turn reinforces the relaxing while running aspect of training.
In my early to mid-fifties I began running farther and easier than ever, which came as quite a surprise as I had come through two episodes of cancer and 3 heart attacks during the previous 15 years, with the second episode with cancer involving a stage 4+ tumour surrounding my spinal cord and extending into the bone and muscles of my left hip and thigh--and being told I was going to lose that leg.
Yet training at the gym and on the roads led me to becoming as fit as I had ever been and running farther and easier than ever.
What had changed was my mind set, as I was now running for fun rather than as training for other sports, and I reminded myself that I was doing something I was told I would never do again as I began each run.
Mind and body, one and the same.
